translations.text: 1. Epiphanius of Cyprus, On Measures and Weights.
This we offer to you, honorable one, for the sake of the grace about which you asked; let there be remembrance on account of it.
There is [?] a setting forth of the twofold writings: first, of the things created by God, made in the six days.
And certain others, compiled [?] from the holy books, recorded according to later times,
from Adam the first-created down to Theodosius the God-loving, for the third time, and Abundantius the illustrious.
Then further, how many names of heresies, 80, have arisen in the world, and their explanation, with a concise and most excellent understanding concerning each of them,
and how many things God made in the six days of the creation of the world, which you requested and which we write to you.
And they are these. On the first day: 1 — the upper heavens, and on the same first day, the lower ones. 2 — the earth.
3 — the waters, from which come snow, ice, hail, frost and dew; and 4 — the ministering spirits, which are these classes of angels:
the angels who give glory, the angels of the winds that blow, the angels of the clouds and of the mist and of the hail and of the snow and of the frost;
the angels of the sound of thunder and of lightning; the angels of cold and of fire; the angels of winter and of sowing, the angels of spring [?] and of summer;
and all the spirits of his creatures in the heavens and on the earth, those of the abysses and those under the earth.
5: hell and the place of perdition, and the darkness over the abysses of the waters, which was once upon the earth, from which comes the dark evening.
6, 7: night, and the light of day and of dawn. These seven mighty works God made on that first day.
And on the second day: first, the firmament between the waters and the waters. On this day the waters were divided:
part of them rose above the firmament and part of them remained below that firmament, in the midst, upon the whole face of the earth.
This alone God made on the 2nd day. And on the third day: seas, rivers, springs, lakes;
second, seed for sowing; third, plants: trees bearing fruit and without fruit; 4 — forests.
These four mighty works God made on the third day. And on the fourth day: 1 — the sun and 2 — the moon; 3 — the stars.
These three great works God made on the 4th day. And on the fifth day: 1 — the great sea monster.
2 — fish and other creatures in the waters, 3 — winged birds. These God made on that 5th day.
And on the sixth day: 1 — wild beasts, 2 — livestock, 3 — the creeping things of the earth and 4 — man.
These 4 great works God made on the 6th day. And all that God made in the 6 days was 22 works.
And he completed all his work on that sixth day, as many things as are in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and the abysses, in light and darkness and in everything.
And God rested from all his works on that 7th day, and he blessed it and sanctified it.
And he made it known to Moses through an angel that there are 22 patriarchs from Adam to Israel.
"And I will choose for myself from his kindred a people acquired from among all the nations."
These were the heads, and these are the generations of whom the Lord spoke, as follows: Adam, Seth, Enosh, Cainan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah,
Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah (but he did not mention Cainan in the count), Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah, Abraham, Isaac and Israel: altogether 22 generations.
For this reason too there are 22 letters of the Hebrews, which are these. The Hebrew alphabet: א Aleph, ב Beth, ג Gimel, ד Daleth, ה He, ו Vav, ז Zanav, ח Heth,
ט Teth, י Yod, כ Kaph, ל Lamed, מ Mem, נ Nun, ס Samekh, ע Ayin, פ Pe, צ Tsade, ק Qoph, ר Resh, ש Shin, ת Tav. For this reason there are 22 books of the Old Law.
These characters among the Hebrews are in a certain way 27, but they are counted as 22, because five of the letters among them are double:
Kaph is double, and Mem and Nun and Pe and Tsade. In the same way the books too are counted:
1: Abesit, which is the Birth of the World; 2: Elismot, which is called the book of Exoduses; 3: Odoiskra, which is the book of the Levites;
4: Ododabir, which is the book of Numbers; 5: Evedebarim, which is the Second Law; 6: Di-Iesu, which is the book of Joshua son of Nun;
7: Diiob, which is Job; 8: Dasoptim, which is the book of Judges; 9: Dirut, which is the book of Ruth; 10: Sphertelim, which is David;
11: Debdriamia, which is the first book of Remnants; 12: Debdmiamin, which is the second book of Remnants; 13: Dismoel, which is the first book of Kings;
14: Di D[?]t Udismoel, which is the second book of Kings; 15: Dmalakim, which is the third book of Kings; 16: Dmalakim, which is the fourth book of Kings;
17: Dmasalot, which is the book of Proverbs; 18: Tkuelet, which is Ecclesiastes; 19: Siram, which is the Song of Songs;
20: Datariasara, which is the book of the 12 Prophets; 21: Diesaia, which is the book of the prophet Isaiah;
22: Diieremia, which is the book of Jeremiah; 22 [?]: Diezekiel, which is the book of Ezekiel; 24: Didaniel, which is the book of Daniel;
25: Diezdra, which is Ezra; 26: Diazdra, which is the second book of Ezra; 27: Diesther, which is the book of Esther.
There are also other small books, which are called Kinot, which is Lamentation.
This is joined to Jeremiah; it is in excess of that number, and it is joined to Jeremiah, so that I may thus inform you of this number of the books too with a true account.
The manner in which this account is introduced is as follows: the children of the Hebrews divide the books of the Old Law into four and into five.
They arrange the books of Moses as a group of five, for they arranged the subsequent ones in the same way as well. These are the books:
the book of Births, the book of Exoduses, the book of the Levites, the book of Numbers, the book of the Second Law. As the second group of five, the stichera, which are these books:
Job, David, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs. And the Wisdom of Solomon and Sirach are also stichera, and they are useful;
those of the Aron, which means of the ark, but the Hebrews did not place them with the Old Law.
As the third group of five, the books of the Prophets, which are these books of the 12 prophets:
Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, who began to prophesy before Ezekiel,
and lived a long time in his life and reached as far as the second year of King Darius, who was before the first year of King Cyrus.
After the times of these prophets, Haggai prophesied at the beginning of the second building of the temple in Jerusalem.
Zechariah also prophesied, forty-six days after Haggai, concerning the completion of the building of the temple.
In those times Malachi also prophesied. And these twelve prophets were written down together.
As a fourth pentad they established the book that is called Dekthobin, which is translated "written."
These books are: Joshua son of Nun, the first book; Judges is joined to the same, and Ruth, because that one letter, namely kaph, is double;
1 and 2 Remnants (Chronicles), because mem is double. And the first and second books of Kings, because nun is double;
3 and 4 Kings, because pe is double. These are the four pentads, which are counted as 20 books; they are 24 heads in number, because those 4 letters are double.
After these 4 pentads, the 21st: the first and second books of Ezra are counted as one book among the Hebrews, because
tsade too is counted as double, which makes 26 heads, told in minute detail.
The book of Esther is counted as the 22nd and is found to be the 27th head. These 22 are found plain [?] and are counted in many different ways, on account of the 22 works
that God made in the six days of the creation of the world; on account of the 22 generations from Adam to Israel; on account of the 22 letters from alef to tav;
and on account of the 22 books from Genesis to Esther.
And it became a measure: the Hebrews call 22 xestes a mod. The Greeks translated mod and likewise give it the name mod.
In the same way the Egyptians give it the name met; in the same way the Assyrians and Arabs likewise give it the name mod, which is translated "confession," that is, modim.
If the mod is not filled up, it is not acknowledged to be full.
And in another place too you will find the interpretation to be twofold. For it is also called gnomon, which is a measure;
it is also given the name confession, and confessed, and confessor: the number of those works of God from the beginning, the bringing in of those 22 letters of the word,
through which the Law came to us, and by God's teaching everything became a name for us; from which the Law and the mysteries within it Christ Jesus, at his coming, attested and revealed to us.
He came and by the Gospel filled up for us the measure of life from that mod, that is, of confession.
Everyone who confesses to him shall be clothed with life from him, by that measure of holiness, for the Hebrews say
that it is 22 xestes, counted according to the earlier mention, which are spoken of in many ways, for many other peoples either added to
or took away from the measure that was truly counted by the Hebrews; but it was also found among the Romans, according to their language.
The mod is called a measure, just as among the Hebrews they teach a child alef in learning, and among the Greeks alpha was found for inquiry and is so named.
But I learned from the Hebrews; they clearly found it in another language as well.
They also divide David into five books. The first runs from the first psalm, which is "Esria" [Ashrei], which is translated:
"Blessed is the man who [?] has gone" up to the one [number missing ?] whose beginning is: "Er meskil al dal oebion" [Ashrei maskil el dal], which is:
"Blessed is he who considers the poor." But Aquila said: "Blessed is [?] to give a good form." The second book: 41, whose beginning is:
"Kial taarog, alafisimain" [Ke-ayyal ta'arog al afiqe mayim], which is translated: "As the hart longs [?]", up to 71, whose beginning is:
"Eloin masfatak lamel ekte" [Elohim mishpatekha la-melekh ten], which is translated: "O God, give your judgment to the king." The third book: 72, whose beginning is:
"Ak bot iel eliom" [Akh tov le-Israel Elohim], which is translated: "How good is the God of Israel to [?] in heart", up to 88, whose beginning is:
"Esdi Adonai lulam asis", which translates as: "Of your mercies, O Lord, let me sing forever."
And as the fourth book, psalm 89, whose beginning is: "Adonai maon ata aiata lanu", which translates as: "Lord, you have been a refuge for us."
[?] — up to 105, whose beginning is: "Udula adonai kitof kelula misdo" [Hodu la-Adonai ki tov ki le-olam hasdo], which is translated:
"Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good." Those psalms have Alleluia. The fifth book: psalm 106, whose beginning is:
"Ud ula Adonai kitob kilul amisdo", which likewise translates as: "Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good"
up to the end, up to the fiftieth psalm, whose beginning is: "Aleluel bakadis", which translates as:
"Praise God in his holy places." That one too is an Alleluia. At the 150th psalm they set the book right.
For the Hebrews make the end of each book of those five books of psalms at the end of that psalm.
The hymn is the end of the book: "Mistobarok Adonai eloi ieli mealo aod laula aminoamin", which translates as:
"Blessed is the Lord God of Israel from now on and forever. So be it, so be it."
This is where each of those same five books ends, which is written at the end of the 40th psalm and of the 71st and of the 88th and of the 105th.
But of the hundred and fiftieth -- "Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, so be it, so be it.
Let every soul praise the Lord", which is said in Hebrew: "Kohannes samate iel telula".
"Alelula" is said for "praise". "Al" is said for "the Lord". And here ends the matter of this Hebrew [?] psalter.
